title: The "Last N Days" Query Needs a Date Index
description: A 'last N days' query with no date index scans all history; index the timestamp so the >= cutoff becomes a range seek to the newest rows. Why it matters: "show recent activity" is one of the most frequently run queries in any system, and it's exactly the kind of query that quietly degrades as history accumulates.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson reinforces the range-index idea from earlier, this time with an open-ended date filter — "everything since some cutoff time" — a pattern that shows up constantly in real applications (recent activity, recent orders, recent logins) and that people sometimes assume doesn't need an index because "it's not an exact match."

Why does this happen? `WHERE LoginAt >= @cutoff` is a range, just like `BETWEEN`, just open on one end. Without an index on `LoginAt`, SQL Server has no way to know which rows qualify without checking every single row's timestamp against the cutoff — there's no shortcut to "everything after this point in time" if nothing is stored in time order.

Picture a security log where entries are stapled together in whatever order they happened to be printed, not sorted by time. If someone asks "show me every login since Tuesday at noon," you'd have to flip through every single page checking its timestamp. Now imagine the same log sorted strictly by time — you could flip straight to Tuesday noon and read everything from that point to the end, ignoring everything before it entirely. That's exactly what an index on a date column gives you for an open-ended "since this time" query: a single jump to the starting point, then a fast read forward, instead of a full sweep of the whole log.

## Scenario
A security screen shows recent logins: everything since a cutoff timestamp. `Logins` has no index on `LoginAt`, so this "last few days" query reads all 300,000 rows every time it runs.

## Why it's slow
`WHERE LoginAt >= @cutoff` is an open-ended **range**. With no index on the date column, the only option is a **Clustered Index Scan** — read the entire table and keep the rows past the cutoff. This is one of the most common queries in any app, and unindexed it gets slower as history grows.

## What to look for
- A Clustered Index Scan for a query that only wants the newest slice of rows.
- Cost that rises with total history, not with how many recent rows match.

## The concept
Index the timestamp you filter and sort on. A nonclustered index on `LoginAt` keeps rows in chronological order, so `>=` a cutoff becomes a **range Index Seek** straight to the recent tail. Date/time columns used for "recent", "between", and "order by newest" queries are almost always worth an index.
hints: There's no index on LoginAt, so the whole table is scanned to find recent rows.
A date index keeps rows in time order, turning >= cutoff into a range seek to the newest rows.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Logins_LoginAt ON Logins(LoginAt) INCLUDE (UserId); then re-run.
